topic: amd silently removes ryzen cpu memory encryption
headline_marked: [[AMD silently removes memory encryption]] from consumer Ryzen CPUs, leaving users vulnerable to physical attacks
headline: AMD silently removes memory encryption from consumer Ryzen CPUs, leaving users vulnerable to physical attacks
summary: A critical security feature, Transparent Secure Memory Encryption (TSME), has vanished from non-Pro Ryzen chips after a firmware update, with AMD engineers going radio silent on the change.
details: AMD has quietly removed Transparent Secure Memory Encryption (TSME) from its consumer Ryzen CPUs, potentially exposing users to physical data siphoning attacks. This critical security feature was previously available on lower-end chips but is now missing after newer AGESA firmware.

A months-long investigation, tracked on GitHub by Ben Kilpatrick, confirmed TSME's disappearance from non-Pro AMD CPUs. When pressed for answers, an AMD engineer abruptly ended discussions, stating, "My apologies, but I don't have any more information to share on this topic."

TSME encrypts data stored in memory, protecting against physical exploits. AMD initially extended this feature from high-end to lower-end CPUs, making its availability a given for consumer chip users.

AMD's only public statement, outside of the GitHub thread, was an email response clarifying TSME "is a security feature only applied to PRO CPUs." This is the first time the company has publicly restricted TSME to Pro chips, despite its long-standing presence on consumer models.

The removal is concerning because it's completely undetectable on Windows machines and requires significant technical effort to identify on Linux. This means users are largely unaware that their security posture has changed.

Ben Kilpatrick, a "privacy-conscious Linux hobbyist," discovered the change when his Host Security ID (HSI) audit reported TSME was no longer supported on his Ryzen 7 9700X, despite being enabled in BIOS.

Initial inquiries to MSI, his motherboard manufacturer, and AMD's public engineering GitHub repository yielded no clear answers. AMD engineers advised re-enabling BIOS options or contacting the motherboard vendor, indicating they were also in the dark.

After Kilpatrick pressed MSI, their engineers conducted tests, confirming that consumer Ryzen chips had TSME enabled with older firmware but showed it as "not supported" with newer AGESA 1.2.7.0. Pro versions maintained the feature regardless of firmware.

The core question remains whether this is an intentional policy decision by AMD to reserve TSME for Pro chips, or an unintentional regression introduced in the AGESA 1.2.7.0 firmware. The silicon itself appears capable of running the feature.

topic: chinese memory brands adopt domestic ddr5 chips
headline_marked: [[Chinese memory brands ditch Samsung and Micron for homegrown CXMT and YMTC silicon]] — Corsair, HP, and Dell already adopting Ch
headline: Chinese memory brands ditch Samsung and Micron for homegrown CXMT and YMTC silicon — Corsair, HP, and Dell already adopting Ch
summary: Major brands like Corsair, HP, and Dell are now adopting China-produced DDR5 chips from CXMT, indicating a significant shift away from traditional suppliers like Samsung and Micron in the memory market.
details: A growing number of Chinese memory vendors are shifting their allegiance from global giants like Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix to domestic producers such as CXMT (ChangXin Memory Technologies) and YMTC (Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp.). This move is largely driven by government backing and a strategic push for technological self-sufficiency within China.

Unlike foreign chipmakers who prioritize maximizing profits from data centers and the AI boom, Chinese chipmakers focus on supplying local companies. This approach helps maintain relatively stable supply and pricing for memory chips and NAND within China, shielding the market from the steep premiums charged by the "Big Three" global memory giants.

Nelson Duann, Senior Vice President at Silicon Motion, noted that China's market is distinct due to its domestic NAND and DRAM makers. He explained that these companies, supported by the government, have a responsibility to help maintain the health of the local market, unlike foreign suppliers who can allocate most of their supply to the highest-return opportunities.

Chinese memory brands Gloway and KingBank have recently unveiled new DDR5 memory modules that prominently feature domestic 24Gb (3GB) memory chips. Utilizing a standard eight-die configuration, these companies can produce 24GB memory modules, which can then be assembled into dual- or quad-DIMM kits for capacities of 48GB or 96GB.

The adoption of Chinese memory chips, particularly CXMT's DDR5, is now extending beyond China's borders. Corsair has already integrated CXMT DDR5 into some memory kits within its Vengeance lineup, and major players like HP and Dell have begun qualifying CXMT memory kits for use in their products.

Despite U.S. export controls limiting access to advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography tools, CXMT has made significant progress using trailing-edge deep ultraviolet (DUV) chipmaking tools. Their current flagship 16nm (G4) manufacturing process produces DDR5 and LPDDR5X chips, which are now featured in memory kits from Corsair, Gloway, and KingBank.
